finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id deletes the report without enforcing the delete grant because authorize() is called without await, so its denial is an unhandled rejection and the handler continues.
finding.source: Request path parameter :id (server.js:19, req.params.id) and caller identity req.user (server.js:5, from req.session.user), both supplied by the HTTP client.

trace.note: req.user is set from req.session.user with no guard.
db.reports.get(req.params.id) loads the report; attacker chooses the id.
authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returns a promise immediately.
Inside authorize, db.grants is awaited; a denial sets err.status=403 and throws, but the throw only rejects the un-awaited promise.
Delete executes regardless of the grant result.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() grant check at server.js:9-16 runs but its result is discarded. The PUT route at server.js:27 uses await and is correct, so the missing await is the defect. No try/catch or error middleware in the file. No session/auth gate before the route.

verdict.guard_found: none. The authorize() grant check at server.js:9-16 is real, but its rejection is never observed by the DELETE handler because the call at server.js:20 has no await, so the delete at server.js:21 runs regardless. No try/catch, error middleware, or session gate exists in server.js. The PUT route at server.js:27 does await and is not affected.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the delete at server.js:21 proceeds even when the grant check throws at server.js:14. However, the only file in the directory is server.js, and nothing in it sets req.session (server.js:5), so every request would throw a TypeError there and never reach the handler; reachability by an authenticated user depends on session middleware that is not in the provided code, so this cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: An anonymous or session-less request can delete any report, and the resulting unhandled promise rejections can crash the Node process (DoS) from a single request.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP request; req.user is undefined when req.session.user is unset (server.js:5). Nonexistent ids also reach null-deref paths via the :id parameter.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove at server.js:21 (data destruction); unhandled rejection at server.js:20 and null dereferences at server.js:20 and server.js:27 (process termination / error).

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; undefined for anonymous callers, no guard.
Loads report by attacker-supplied id; returns null for nonexistent ids, which is not checked.
authorize(undefined, ...) throws TypeError at server.js:10 (user.id) inside async function, becoming an unhandled rejection; handler does not await.
PUT path: null report from db.reports.get is not checked; server.js:27 then dereferences resource.id and throws inside an awaited async handler.

finding.guards_checked: No null check on report (server.js:19, 26). No check that req.user exists (server.js:5). No try/catch or error middleware. Behavior depends on Node version (unhandled rejections terminate by default on Node 15+) and on Express version (Express 4 does not forward async rejections; Express 5 would return 500). The unhandled rejection at server.js:20 occurs under either Express version. Assumes express-session leaves req.session.user unset for anonymous requests, which is not shown in this repository.

verdict.guard_found: The only authorization control is authorize() (server.js:9-16). At server.js:20 it is called as a bare statement without await or try/catch, so its rejection (403 or the TypeError at server.js:10) is discarded and never blocks the delete at server.js:21. No null check exists on report (server.js:19, 26), and there is no error middleware. The line-27 call is awaited, so it does not have this bypass.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the 403 or TypeError is an unhandled rejection and db.reports.remove still runs at server.js:21, letting any caller that reaches the route delete a report even without a grant. The attacker can be anonymous (req.user undefined at server.js:5) or any authenticated user lacking the grant, and the only control is ineffective. Caveats: express-session is not in this repo, so the anonymous case depends on it leaving req.session.user unset; db is not defined here, so the null return from db.reports.get is assumed; and on Node 15+ the crash may interrupt the delete in flight, making the deletion itself racy while the bypass remains.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update with no field allowlist, so a caller with write on one report may be able to modify protected fields such as ownership or grants if the schema allows.
finding.source: JSON request body (req.body), parsed by express.json() at server.js:3, supplied by the authenticated HTTP client.

trace.note: express.json() parses the body into req.body with no schema.
Loads the target report by attacker-supplied id.
await authorize(req.user, 'write', report) grants write on this report only.
Whole req.body forwarded to db.reports.update; no allowlist or validation in this file.

finding.guards_checked: Write grant check at server.js:27 is awaited and correct. No field allowlist, schema validation, or stripping of id/owner/grant fields in this file. db layer not in repository, so whether update filters columns is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: authorize(req.user, "write", report) at server.js:27 is awaited and throws a 403 when the write grant is missing, so only a user with write on this report reaches the sink. No field allowlist, schema validation, or stripping of id/owner/grant fields exists in server.js (lines 25-30).
verdict.reason: The trace in server.js:3, 26-28 is accurate and the write check at server.js:27 is effective, but whether db.reports.update at server.js:28 lets the body overwrite ownership or grant fields depends on the db layer, which is not in the repository, so the mass-assignment claim cannot be decided from this code. (Separately, server.js:20 calls authorize without await, so the DELETE route at lines 18-23 likely skips its check; that is outside this finding.)
